title: Appeals Court Rules 2022 $1.7 Trillion Federal Spending Package Passed Unconstitutionally
snippet: A federal appeals court ruled that the U.S. House violated the Constitution's Quorum Clause by using pandemic-era proxy voting to pass a massive 2022 omnibus funding bill.
content:
NEW ORLEANS — A federal appeals court ruled Friday that the U.S. House of Representatives acted unconstitutionally when it passed a $1.7 trillion omnibus spending package in late 2022 by relying on pandemic-era proxy voting rules.

In a tight 9-8 decision, the conservative-leaning 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld an injunction secured by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. The ruling prevents the federal government from enforcing a specific component of the legislation—the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act—against the state of Texas.

Constitutional Quorum at Center of Ruling

The core of the legal challenge rests on the House's temporary proxy voting system, established in May 2020 under former Speaker Nancy Pelosi to allow legislative business to continue during the COVID-19 pandemic. When the multi-trillion-dollar funding bill came up for a vote in December 2022, 226 House members cast their votes by proxy. The legislation cleared the chamber in a 225-201 vote before being signed into law by President Joe Biden.

Writing for the majority, U.S. Circuit Judge Cory Wilson, an appointee of former President Donald Trump, determined that the U.S. Constitution's Quorum Clause requires lawmakers to be physically present in the chamber to conduct business.

"While the chambers of the legislature have much discretion regarding their rules of procedure, the Quorum Clause’s constraints on congressional power cannot be circumvented by congressional fiat," Wilson wrote in the opinion.

Dissent Points to Inconsistencies

Despite the broad conclusion that the spending package was unconstitutionally enacted, the 5th Circuit issued a narrow remedy. The court only blocked the Department of Justice and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission from enforcing the workplace pregnancy protections against Texas state agencies.

The decision drew sharp criticism from dissenting judges on the panel. U.S. Circuit Judge James Graves, an appointee of former President Barack Obama, condemned the ruling as "illogical, inexplicable, and invalid."

Graves stated in his dissent that the majority manufactured a physical-presence requirement not explicitly written into the Constitution. He further questioned the decision to strike down enforcement of a single provision while leaving the remainder of the multitrillion-dollar statute untouched.

The proxy voting rule was formally discarded by House Republicans after taking control of the chamber in early 2023. Neither the Department of Justice nor Paxton's office immediately issued public comments following Friday's ruling.
